concepts.name: EXIM Bank: Establishment, Ownership and Legal Status
key_dimensions: Established under Export-Import Bank of India Act, 1981 — NOT under Companies Act or Banking Regulation Act
100% Government of India owned — distinction from SIDBI, NABARD which have mixed ownership
Commenced operations on March 1, 1982 — took over international financing operations from IDBI
Statutory body vs. scheduled bank classification — EXIM Bank is NOT a scheduled commercial bank under RBI Act Second Schedule

concepts.name: EXIM Bank's Mandate vs. ECGC: Functional Overlap and Distinction
key_dimensions: EXIM Bank provides financing (loans, guarantees, equity) while ECGC provides credit insurance and risk cover — common UPSC confusion point
ECGC covers risk of non-payment; EXIM Bank directly funds exporters/importers
Both promote exports but through completely different financial instruments
ECGC is under Ministry of Commerce; EXIM Bank is under Ministry of Finance — jurisdictional trap

concepts.name: EXIM Bank's Regulatory Oversight and Supervisory Framework
key_dimensions: Regulated by RBI under Export-Import Bank of India Act — NOT under Banking Regulation Act 1949
Classified as an All India Financial Institution (AIFI) alongside NABARD, NHB, SIDBI
RBI prescribes prudential norms, capital adequacy separately for AIFIs vs. commercial banks
Not subject to CRR/SLR requirements like commercial banks — key distinction for Prelims

concepts.name: Lines of Credit (LOC): Mechanism and Strategic Significance
key_dimensions: LOC is EXIM Bank's flagship instrument — extends credit to foreign governments, central banks, financial institutions to finance Indian exports
Sovereign-backed LOC vs. commercial LOC — risk profile and concessional interest rate differences
LOC supports India's development diplomacy — linkage to Indian Technical and Economic Cooperation (ITEC) and foreign policy
UPSC trap: LOC beneficiary country uses funds to procure goods/services from India — tied aid concept

concepts.name: EXIM Bank's Buyer's Credit vs. Supplier's Credit
key_dimensions: Buyer's Credit: EXIM Bank lends directly to foreign buyer to purchase Indian goods — risk on foreign entity
Supplier's Credit: EXIM Bank lends to Indian exporter who in turn extends credit to foreign buyer — risk on Indian entity
Distinction critical for understanding who bears exchange rate and default risk
Both facilitate deferred payment exports — important for capital goods and project exports

concepts.name: EXIM Bank and Project Exports: Turnkey and Construction Contracts
key_dimensions: EXIM Bank specifically mandated to finance project exports — unique compared to commercial banks
Covers turnkey contracts, construction contracts, technical services exports — distinction from merchandise exports
Overseas Investment Finance — supports Indian companies setting up joint ventures/wholly owned subsidiaries abroad
Linkage to Make in India and Aatmanirbhar Bharat — financing Indian engineering exports

concepts.name: EXIM Bank's Role in Financing Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs)
key_dimensions: EXIM Bank extends credit lines to domestic banks/NBFCs for on-lending to MSMEs for export purposes — two-tier lending model
Distinction from direct lending — EXIM Bank not a retail lender for MSMEs
MSME cluster development financing — geographic concentration of export-oriented industries
Overlap with SIDBI mandate — UPSC may test which institution has primary MSME mandate (SIDBI) vs. export-specific MSME support (EXIM)

concepts.name: EXIM Bank's Equity Participation and Overseas Investment
key_dimensions: EXIM Bank can take equity stake in overseas ventures — not just debt financing, distinguishing it from purely credit institutions
Supports Indian companies acquiring foreign companies or setting up subsidiaries — strategic outbound FDI facilitation
Equity + debt blending creates 'risk capital' for emerging market projects
Linkage to FEMA provisions on overseas direct investment — regulatory framework overlap

concepts.name: EXIM Bank's Concessional Financing Scheme (CFS) for Government-Backed Projects
key_dimensions: CFS provides concessional loans for projects in developing countries — funded by Government of India budgetary support
Distinction from commercial LOC — CFS carries sovereign guarantee and lower interest rates (often below market)
Used for development projects in Africa, South Asia under India's foreign assistance framework
CFS vs. ODA (Official Development Assistance) — India does not officially categorize as ODA but functionally similar

concepts.name: EXIM Bank's Resource Mobilization: Borrowing Powers and Instruments
key_dimensions: EXIM Bank raises funds through bonds, notes, commercial paper in domestic and international markets — NOT through deposits from public
Can borrow from RBI, Government of India, international capital markets — multiple funding windows
Foreign currency bonds (Masala Bonds denominated in INR raised overseas) — exchange rate risk on investor
Capital adequacy maintained as per RBI norms for AIFIs — Basel framework applicability

concepts.name: EXIM Bank vs. NABARD vs. NHB vs. SIDBI: Comparative AIFI Framework
key_dimensions: All four are All India Financial Institutions under RBI supervision — but have sector-specific mandates
NABARD: Agriculture/rural; NHB: Housing; SIDBI: MSMEs; EXIM: International trade — clean sectoral division
UPSC trap: Which AIFIs can refinance commercial banks? NABARD and NHB primarily refinance; EXIM primarily lends directly
Ownership structure difference: NHB (RBI transferred stake to GOI in 2019), NABARD (GOI + RBI), SIDBI (GOI + financial institutions), EXIM (100% GOI)

concepts.name: EXIM Bank and India's Foreign Policy: Geopolitical Lending Patterns
key_dimensions: LOC portfolio heavily concentrated in Africa, South Asia, ASEAN — mirrors India's Neighbourhood First and Act East policies
EXIM Bank as a soft power instrument — infrastructure financing creates economic dependency and goodwill
Comparison with China's policy banks (China Development Bank, China EXIM Bank) — debt trap diplomacy debate
India's EXIM Bank LOCs carry conditionality of 75% Indian content — protects domestic industry, a key policy design feature

concepts.name: 75% Indian Content Requirement in EXIM Bank LOCs
key_dimensions: At least 75% of contract value must be sourced from India — ensures LOCs benefit Indian exporters directly
This conditionality distinguishes India's LOCs from IMF/World Bank financing which is untied
Creates tension between development effectiveness (recipient country's needs) and India's export promotion goal
Recent relaxations and exceptions — for strategic partner countries, critical infrastructure projects

concepts.name: EXIM Bank's Role in Export Credit Refinance (ECR) — Historical Context
key_dimensions: RBI used to provide Export Credit Refinance facility to banks — EXIM Bank was a channel for export credit ecosystem
RBI phased out ECR facility in 2015 — liquidity support to exporters now through normal LAF/MSF
UPSC trap: ECR was provided by RBI to commercial banks, not directly by EXIM Bank — institutional clarity critical
Post-ECR withdrawal, EXIM Bank's direct lending role became more prominent for large project/LOC financing

concepts.name: EXIM Bank's Technology and Innovation Financing: Emerging Mandates
key_dimensions: Financing export of defence equipment under Make in India — new mandate aligned with Defence Export Policy 2020
Support for green exports — renewable energy equipment financing for overseas projects
Pharmaceutical export financing — critical during COVID for vaccine diplomacy (Vaccine Maitri)
Digital exports and IT services — EXIM Bank exploring financing for services sector unlike traditional goods focus

concepts.name: EXIM Bank's Guarantee Products: Performance and Financial Guarantees
key_dimensions: Issues guarantees on behalf of Indian exporters to foreign buyers/lenders — contingent liability, not direct loan
Performance guarantee: assures contract completion; Financial guarantee: assures repayment
Distinction from ECGC guarantee — ECGC guarantees banks against exporter default; EXIM guarantees foreign party against Indian exporter's non-performance
Counter-guarantee arrangements — EXIM Bank may take counter-guarantee from Indian exporter before issuing guarantee

concepts.name: EXIM Bank and Special Economic Zones (SEZs) / Export Oriented Units (EOUs)
key_dimensions: Preferential financing for SEZ units and EOUs — lower interest rates, longer tenors
Linkage with Foreign Trade Policy (FTP) — EXIM Bank aligns products with FTP incentive schemes
UPSC overlap: SEZ governed by SEZ Act 2005 under Ministry of Commerce; EXIM Bank financing is separate from SEZ tax incentives
Export Promotion Capital Goods (EPCG) scheme interaction — EXIM Bank can finance capital goods imports under EPCG

concepts.name: EXIM Bank's Governance Structure: Board Composition and Management
key_dimensions: Board includes representatives from RBI, Ministry of Finance, Ministry of Commerce, FIEO, and independent directors — multi-stakeholder representation
MD & CEO appointed by Government of India — political economy of appointments
Distinction from commercial bank boards which must have majority independent directors under RBI corporate governance norms
Parliamentary oversight: EXIM Bank accounts placed before Parliament — accountability mechanism

concepts.name: Non-Performing Assets (NPAs) and Risk Management in EXIM Bank's LOC Portfolio
key_dimensions: Sovereign LOCs carry lower NPA risk as repayment backed by foreign government — but sub-sovereign and commercial LOCs carry higher risk
Debt distress in African nations (Zambia, Ethiopia) creates challenges for EXIM Bank's LOC recovery
Provisioning norms for AIFIs — RBI mandates specific provisioning for NPAs in EXIM Bank's books
Debt restructuring under G20 Common Framework — EXIM Bank's exposure affects India's position in multilateral debt negotiations

concepts.name: EXIM Bank's Relationship with Multilateral Development Banks (MDBs)
key_dimensions: Co-financing arrangements with World Bank, ADB, AfDB — EXIM Bank participates in larger infrastructure projects alongside MDBs
EXIM Bank is NOT an MDB — bilateral institution vs. multilateral character is a classic UPSC distinction
New Development Bank (NDB/BRICS Bank) and AIIB — EXIM Bank can complement these institutions in project financing
Difference in conditionalities — MDB loans have governance/environmental conditionalities; EXIM LOCs primarily have Indian content conditionality
